title: The gift of tears
hookLine: holy grief: tears that wash rather than wound

cards: Peter is sitting by a fire in a courtyard, the night Jesus is arrested. Someone says he was with Jesus. He says he doesn't know the man.
It happens again, and again. Then, while he's still speaking, a rooster crows. Luke says the Lord turned, and looked at Peter, and Peter remembers what Jesus told him would happen.
The King James says it in seven words: "And Peter went out, and wept bitterly." You met that night back on day sixty-seven. Those tears weren't the end of Peter's story.
They were closer to a turning point. The Orthodox teachers of prayer have a word for weeping like that, and they call it a gift.

teach.b: Penthos is Greek for mourning, grief. Mourning gets a blessing of its own in the Sermon on the Mount: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted."
In The Ladder of Divine Ascent, a monk called John Climacus gives a whole step to mourning, and gives it a strange name: joy-making mourning. Grief with joy folded inside it. Penthos isn't despair.

Despair looks at what's broken, a harsh word, a wasted year, a friend let down, and says it's hopeless. Penthos grieves the very same thing in the presence of God. One closes a door; the other opens one.
The Psalms know the difference: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy."
Another psalm asks God to keep them: "put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?" Not one wasted.
That's why the teachers call tears a gift, not a skill. You can't manufacture them, and nobody is asked to. They come or they don't, and grief can be dry-eyed too: a quiet ache, a softening heart.
And it isn't only about sin. At the tomb of his friend Lazarus, John's Gospel says it in two words: "Jesus wept." Tears that wound leave a person smaller, ashamed and alone.
Tears that wash leave them lighter, turned back toward God and toward the people they love.

how: Orthodox teachers speak of the gift of tears as something received, not produced; it is tied to repentance, confession and prayer, and they describe it as leading to joy rather than despair.

o: holy grief that washes and turns you toward God
a hopeless sorrow over sins that can't be undone
a monk's vow to weep each day for the world

s: penthos is another word for despair
despair says it's hopeless. penthos grieves in God's presence, and Climacus calls it joy-making.
the teachers say you should force yourself to cry
they call tears a gift. they come or they don't, and a dry-eyed ache counts too.

games.q: you're Peter. the rooster has crowed, and the Lord has turned and looked at you. what do you do?
o: insist again that you never knew him.
slip away and pretend it didn't happen.
games.why: "Peter went out, and wept bitterly." those tears weren't his end: in John's Gospel the risen Jesus meets him again by the sea.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're sorry for, or one loss you've never stopped to grieve, and stay with it without pushing it away or pushing yourself to cry; if tears come, let them, and if they don't, a soft ache counts too.
If you pray, hold it out to God; if not, simply stay with it kindly. And if the grief ever turns into not wanting to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Penthos. Holy grief: mourning that softens rather than crushes, the tears the Orthodox teachers call a gift.

orig.note: Greek for mourning or grief; the Orthodox teachers of prayer speak of it as holy grief.

carryVoice: Your line: tears that wash. Grief, held before God, can open a door. Until tomorrow.
